doc.title: Randy Brecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 12, 2022

title: South Philly jam sessions and the Philly recording scene
summary: Local players at Sunday jam sessions (Savitt, Montana) turned out to be busy session men behind Gamble & Huff and early disco records.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Well just by seeing where musicians played and being on the scene and seeing it was a rough life. Unbeknownst to me though, going back on it, a lot of the Philly cats, who I saw — and I don’t remember the name of the place — there were Sunday afternoon jam sessions in South Philly with some of these names you might know, maybe you wouldn’t, names like Vince Montana; Buddy Savitt, tenor player; Vince was a vibist. John Bonnie, alto saxophone, local cats. And I would always wonder myself, gee, they’re playing here, they probably make fifty bucks, how do they make a living? And unbeknownst to me at the time all these guys were very successful in the local recording business and they had started a lot, they worked with eventually Gamble & Huff and was one huge — I don’t know consortium I guess of guys that were producing records, pop records, R&B, really disco records, a lot of the birth of disco in a way it was through these guys. I had no idea at the time. But upon reading about the Philly history on its website and it said “the most listened to tenor player in the world” and I had just known that he had played with Woody Herman, that’s John Bonnie, and was a great player in that style, and the Lester Youngish, a little more modern style. But here they were on all these rock & roll records. I didn’t know that until way later. It’s really interesting.
Let me go back because you froze up for a minute when you said who was the most listened to tenor player.
Oh I’m sorry, I guess, I hope I have a better connection, his name was Buddy Savitt.

Yeah. And he died pretty young I think, at 52 or 53. Wonderful player though. He’d played with — I guess his main claim to fame was he took Stan Getz’s place with Woody Herman. But lo and behold, like I said, I had no idea. In fact I found a record with all these cats on it where it’s kind of a comedy record where somebody’s narrating and they’re swinging along a couple choruses of blues, and somebody’s saying “here’s the way we want to play,” and then a couple of choruses later, “and here’s the way we have to play” and then they go and do an R&B, and then back and forth as the whole record. But they were on a lot of hit records and I guess that had a big influence subconsciously, even though I didn’t know they were doing that. It’s kind of funny that I didn’t at that time.
